claims.text: The initial non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, metastable solid solution.
The initial alloy has a uniform distribution of Mg and other alloying elements such as Al, Cu, Zn, and Gd.
Thermal or corrosive exposure causes Mg to diffuse and segregate to grain boundaries.
Mg segregation promotes nucleation and growth of coarse Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, particularly at grain boundaries.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates locally depletes protective elements such as Al from grain-boundary regions.
Al would ordinarily contribute to the formation of stable, protective oxides.
Depletion of protective elements at altered grain boundaries creates preferential sites for rapid, non-protective oxide growth.
The grain-boundary chemical and microstructural changes enhance corrosive attack.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, thermally or chemically aged material will have a higher corrosion rate.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, aged material will develop thicker and less protective oxide scales.
The oxide scales produced after aging will be dominated by Mg- and Cu-rich compounds.
Aged samples will show pronounced Mg segregation and resolved Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries.
Annealing at approximately 600°C in air for 100 hours is proposed as a treatment capable of activating diffusion and phase separation.
Prolonged exposure to a 3.5% NaCl solution is proposed as an alternative way to induce phase separation.
The hypothesis is restricted to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with density below 6 g/cm³ and constituent-property differences that predispose them to intermetallic formation.
The controlled experiment compares an as-cast sample set with an otherwise matched sample set annealed at 600°C in air for 100 hours.
The proposed measurements include grain-boundary chemistry, Mg-rich precipitate morphology, corrosion current and impedance, and oxide-scale thickness and phase composition.

The hypothesis is falsified if annealing produces neither significant Mg segregation or Mg-rich grain-boundary precipitation nor a measurable increase in corrosion rate or deterioration of oxide protection.
